ny_flatrock_boulders.blurb: A small, low-key boulder field in the woods southwest of Old Forge in the Adirondacks, with a few short roped lines on little cliffbands. Eleven climbs in all: mostly boulder problems from V0 up to a single V6, with the bulk in the easy-to-moderate range, plus two top-rope pitches. The stone is fine-grained and banded with quartz, and the forest is thick, so expect moss, damp pockets and bugs in summer. One big split boulder sits right by the road, and a swampy low spot holds more blocks that only dry out late in the season. Better as a quick stop than a destination.
ny_flatrock_boulders.parking_note: Small unmarked pull-off lot beside NY 28 south of Old Forge, screened by trees; the first boulders can be seen from the highway.

ny_chatiemac_cliff.blurb: A steep, little-visited cliff on the southeast shoulder of Gore Mountain, deep in the Adirondacks' Indian Lake region. The main face leans past vertical, with plate-like features and pockets on solid overhanging holds. Eleven climbs, nearly all of them bolted: one in the low 5.10s, three at 5.11, three at 5.12 and four at 5.13, so this is a place for strong sport climbers rather than beginners. Routes tend to be short, a few moderately long. Reaching it takes a trail walk followed by a short, rough bushwhack to a path along the base.
ny_chatiemac_cliff.parking_note: Drive Chatiemac Road to the Second Pond trailhead, which has room for only a handful of cars.
ny_chatiemac_cliff.approach: Follow the Second Pond Trail for roughly ten minutes (the trail is blazed and crosses Chatiemac Brook), leave it near a small pointed boulder on the right, push through the woods for about 200 feet to a path, and follow that to the base. Allow around half an hour in total.

ny_cave_wall.blurb: The first wall you meet on the climbers' trail at Hailes Cave South in Thacher State Park, on the Helderberg Escarpment near Voorheesville. Eleven bolted routes on limestone climb the vertical faces beneath and beside a handful of large horizontal roofs wrapped around a small cave. Lengths run from a few bolts to about 90 feet. Grades start in the 5.7 and 5.9 range, but most lines are 5.11 and 5.12 with a couple of 5.13s, so it suits those comfortable on steep, pumpy sport climbing. Shade-leaning, with the morning sun on the wall.

ny_center_of_progress_cliff.blurb: A remote, quiet cliff above Silver Lake in the northern Adirondacks, known for its long traditional lines and, when conditions allow, ice and mixed routes on the shorter cliff to the right. The main wall is organised around a right-facing flake system and a full-length chimney. Eleven rock routes here, mostly trad with three sport lines, running from the 5.7 range through a clustering of 5.9 and 5.10 up to one 5.13. Bring a standard rack and expect to build natural anchors. The setting is wild and self-reliant, with a walk-off back down.
ny_center_of_progress_cliff.parking_note: Pull off along Turnpike Road at the gated logging road that also serves neighbouring Summit Cliff; the cliff is reached on foot from there.

ny_rocky_glen_pond.blurb: A compact bouldering spot beside a pond in Blue Mountain Park at Peekskill, about an hour north of Manhattan. Three main boulders stand to one side of the trail where it meets the water, each with several problems, which makes it an easy place to warm up or to bring newer boulderers. The eleven problems are mostly in the VB to V3 range, with one or two V4s at the top. Some of the easier lines are cracks. The park has several entrances and also holds other small boulder groups a bit farther along its trails.

ny_lower_measles_wall.blurb: The first and widest of the short Measles Walls on Crane Mountain in the Adirondacks, with the trail passing right beneath it. Eleven routes mix trad, sport and a top-rope: a handful of easy lines in the 5.3 to 5.5 range, a couple around 5.8, and five at 5.10. The cliff is pockmarked, with an easy dihedral, tricky slabs and divoted face climbing. It faces south and is short and wooded, so it stays cool in summer and warms once the leaves drop. The left side is wet and mossy; the right of the main drainage is far better. Handy when daylight is short.
